Brill (Scophthalmus rhombus) is a commercially valuable flatfish inhabiting the northeastern Atlantic, and its life-history traits have been characterized through several field and laboratory studies. The maximum total length recorded for this species reaches 75 cm [Li = 75 cm], a size that places it among the larger pleuronectiforms within its range. In contrast, the total length at which individuals attain puberty is considerably smaller, measured at 37 cm [Lp = 37 cm]. This substantial difference between pubertal and ultimate size suggests an extended adult growth phase following the onset of reproduction. Data from captive rearing experiments indicate that the wet weight at birth for newly hatched larvae is approximately 0.00036 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00036 grams], reflecting the tiny egg size of this broadcast spawner. This minimal starting mass imposes a strong selective pressure for rapid larval development and efficient yolk utilization during the early lecithotrophic stage.

Egg incubation and early life stages of Brill occur under specific thermal regimes, with many developmental parameters quantified at a stable temperature of 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C]. Under these conditions, the age at birth, defined as the time from fertilisation to hatching, is approximately 21 days [ab = approximately 21 days] at a temperature of 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C]. This relatively short incubation period is typical of flatfish producing small pelagic eggs. Larvae emerge as yolk-sac larvae and commence exogenous feeding shortly thereafter. The consistent thermal environment used in these measurements reflects the species' preference for cooler temperate waters, and the 11.2 °C benchmark is frequently employed in laboratory investigations to standardise comparisons across studies. The rapid transition from an endotrophic to an exotrophic feeding mode is critical for larval survival, as the yolk reserves are exhausted quickly at this temperature.

This corresponds to an annual fecundity that underpins the species' iteroparous strategy. The wet weight at puberty, recorded at 575.5 grams [Wwp = 575.5 grams], represents the body mass threshold at which vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis become active. Individuals below this mass typically show no signs of gonadal recrudescence, indicating that a critical energetic reserve must be accumulated before reproductive investment begins.

The ultimate wet weight attained by Brill reaches 4800 grams [Wwi = 4800 grams], a value consistent with allometric growth equations derived from length-weight relationships in this species. This substantial adult body mass is supported by a benthic diet of crustaceans and small fish, allowing individuals to accumulate significant lipid reserves. The contrast between the mass at puberty, 575.5 grams [Wwp = 575.5 grams], and the ultimate mass highlights a prolonged post-pubertal growth phase during which somatic investment continues alongside reproductive effort. Longevity records for Brill indicate a maximum lifespan of 38 years [am = 38 years] when maintained at 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C], a notably extended duration for a flatfish of this body size. This exceptional lifespan, spanning nearly four decades, allows for multiple spawning seasons across an individual's lifetime. The 38-year (38 years) [am = 38 years] maximum contrasts with the relatively modest ultimate total length of 75 cm [Li = 75 cm], suggesting that growth slows considerably after sexual maturity while somatic maintenance remains robust at a temperature of 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C]. Such a life-history strategy—slow growth, substantial longevity, and iteroparity—is well suited to the variable recruitment environments of temperate continental shelves, where reproductive success in any single year may be low but cumulative lifetime output can be substantial.
